core: Defining social class: a group sharing similar economic position and life chances (working definition, attributed)
Class as position: income, wealth, education, occupation, and the honest note that class is multidimensional
U.S. class categories: upper, middle, working, lower/poor — descriptive, no value judgments
Class and life chances: class shapes opportunities and outcomes (Weber's concept, attributed data, original example)
Class consciousness: awareness of class position, attributed to Marxist theory, stated simply
Social mobility: movement between classes, with the honest note that mobility is limited for many
supporting: Multidimensionality: status consistency; Weber's distinction between class (economic position) and status (prestige)
Measurement: Pew Research Center income tiers defined against the national median household income
Mobility types: upward, downward, intergenerational, intragenerational, structural
One-line context: class systems sit within social stratification and are open systems
Class traits as markers of class (descriptive only)

claims.claim: A social class is a group of people who share a similar social status based on factors like wealth, income, education, and occupation; class is a socioeconomic position within an open class system, not a fixed legal rank.

Class position has several dimensions: income (money earned from work or investments), wealth (the value of money and assets a person has, including inheritance), education, and occupation; sociologists treat class as multidimensional.

Sociologists generally identify three broad levels of class in the United States — upper, middle, and lower — with many subcategories; the label 'working class' is applied to people in manual, service, and production jobs, sometimes treated as the upper portion of the lower tier.

Pew Research Center classifies households by income relative to the national median (adjusted for household size): lower income below two-thirds of the median, middle income between two-thirds and double the median, upper income above double the median.

The share of U.S. adults living in middle-income households fell from 61% in 1971 to 51% in 2019; over the same period the upper-income share rose from 14% to 20% and the lower-income share rose from 25% to 29%.

Life chances — the opportunities a person's social position provides to improve their quality of life — is a concept introduced by Max Weber; life chances are positively correlated with socioeconomic status.

Class shapes outcomes at the group level: more than 40% of Americans raised in the bottom quintile of the family income ladder remain there as adults, and about 70% remain below the middle; an absolute majority (84%) exceed their parents' family income; a four-year degree is associated with upward mobility from the bottom.

Class consciousness is the self-understanding of members of a social class; the concept is closely associated with Marxist theory, in which workers first become conscious of shared grievances (a class 'in itself') and then develop awareness of themselves as a class opposed to the bourgeoisie (a class 'for itself').

Social mobility is the ability to change positions within a social stratification system; sociologists distinguish upward, downward, intergenerational (between generations of a family), intragenerational (within a lifetime), and structural (society-wide) mobility.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many classes does the United States have?
positions: Pew Research Center measures three income tiers (lower, middle, upper) defined against the national median household income
Sociologists generally describe three broad classes (upper, middle, lower) with many subcategories, and some schemes add a distinct working class or an underclass
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the categories descriptively — upper, middle, working, lower/poor — and states plainly that researchers draw the boundaries differently. No single official scheme exists.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Did Karl Marx himself coin 'class consciousness'?
positions: Textbooks commonly credit the concept of class consciousness to Marx
Britannica notes that Marx intimated the concept in his characterization of the working class but did not articulate a full theory; later Marxists such as György Lukács developed it
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes class consciousness to Marxist theory and states Marx's role simply (awareness of class position, associated with Marx), avoiding the stronger claim that Marx authored a finished theory.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much social mobility is there in the United States?
positions: Absolute mobility is common: 84% of Americans have higher family incomes than their parents (Pew Charitable Trusts)
Relative mobility from the bottom is limited: more than 40% of those raised in the bottom quintile remain there as adults, and about 70% remain below the middle
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports both findings: most people move up in absolute terms, yet movement out of the bottom is limited — that two-sided picture is the lesson's honest note on mobility.
